topic.name: The Area Bounded by Two Polar Curves

question.text: Find the shaded area that lies between the polar curves $r=2(1+\sin\theta)$ and $r=1+\sin\theta,$ as shown above.
question.explanation:
First, we find the values of $\theta$ for which the two curves intersect:

\begin{align*} 2(1+\sin\theta) &= 1+\sin\theta \\[3pt] 2+2\sin\theta &= 1+\sin\theta \\[3pt] \sin\theta &= -1 \end{align*}

This gives us two solutions for $\theta \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]\mathbin{:}$ \[ \theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \]

To determine the inner function and the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

The arrow

  • enters the region through the inner function $r=1+\sin\theta,$ and

  • leaves through the outer function $r=2(1+\sin\theta).$

To find the area, we use the formula

\[ A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \Big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{outer}} \big]^2 - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{inner}} \big]^2 \Big) \:\textrm{d}\theta, \]

where

$\qquad$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \quad$ and $\quad \theta_2=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}.$

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} A &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} \left( (2(1+\sin\theta))^2 - (1+\sin\theta)^2 \right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \int_{-\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} \left( 1+2\sin\theta + \sin^2\theta \right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \left( \theta\Bigr|_{-\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} - 2\cos\theta\Bigr|_{-\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} +\dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} \left( 1 - \cos(2\theta) \right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \left( \left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right) - 2(0-0) + \dfrac{1}{2}\theta\Bigr|_{-\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} - \dfrac{1}{4} \sin(2\theta)\Bigr|_{-\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \left( 2\pi + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right) - \dfrac{1}{4}(0-0) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \left( 2\pi + \pi \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{9\pi}{2}. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Area of the Region Bounded by Two Polar Curves

question.text: Which of the following gives the area of the shaded region that lies between the polar curves $r=2\sin\theta$ and $r=1,$ as shown above?
question.explanation:
First, we find the values of $\theta$ for which the two curves intersect:

\begin{align*} 2\sin\theta &= 1 \\[3pt] \sin\theta &= \dfrac 1 2 \end{align*}

We have two solutions:

$\qquad$ $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$

To determine the inner function and the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

The arrow

  • enters the region through the inner function $r=1,$ and

  • leaves through the outer function $r=2\sin\theta.$

To find the area, we use the formula

\[ A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \Big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{outer}} \big]^2 - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{inner}} \big]^2 \Big) \:\textrm{d}\theta, \]

where

$\qquad$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{\pi}{6} \quad$ and $\quad \theta_2=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}.$

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} A &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\bigl( (2\sin\theta)^2 - 1^2 \bigr) \, \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6} \left( 4\sin^2\theta-1\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta\,. \end{align*}

example.title: Writing an Integral Expression For the Area Bounded by Two Polar Curves

question.text: Find the total area of the shaded region that lies between the polar curves $r=1+\cos(3\theta)$ and $r=1,$ as shown above.
question.explanation:
Consider the mostright petal along $x$-axis. First, we find the values of $\theta$ for which the two curves intersect: \begin{align*} 1+\cos(3\theta) &= 1 \\[5pt] \cos(3\theta) &= 0. \end{align*}

This gives us two solutions for $3\theta \in [-\pi,\pi]\mathbin{:}$ \[ 3\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta= -\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{\pi}{6} \]

To determine which is the inner function and which is the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

The arrow

  • enters the region through the inner function $r=1,$ and

  • leaves through the outer function $r=1+\cos(3\theta).$

To find the area, we use the formula

\[ A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \Big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{outer}} \big]^2 - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{inner}} \big]^2 \Big) \:\textrm{d}\theta, \]

where

$\qquad$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \quad$ and $\quad \theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} A_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \left( (1+\cos(3\theta)))^2 - 1^2 \right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \left( 1+2\cos(3\theta) + \cos^2(3\theta) - 1 \right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \left(2\cos(3\theta) + \cos^2(3\theta)\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \left( 2\cos(3\theta)+\dfrac{1}{2}(1+\cos(6\theta) \right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{2}{3}\sin(3\theta) \Bigr|_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} + \dfrac{1}{2} \theta\Bigr|_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} + \dfrac{1}{12}\sin(6\theta)\Bigr|_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6} \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[ \left( \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3} \right) +\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right) + \dfrac{1}{12} \left(0\right) \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{\pi}{12}. \end{align*}

Finally, the total shaded area is \[ A = 3A_1 = 3\left( \dfrac{2}{3}+\dfrac{\pi}{12} \right)=2+\dfrac{\pi}{4}. \]

example.title: Finding the Area of the Region Bounded by Two Polar Curves With Multiple Intersections

question.text: Find the area $A$ of the shaded region that lies between the polar curves $r=1-\cos\theta$ and $r=\cos\theta,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, we find the values of $\theta$ for which the two curves intersect: \begin{align*} 1-\cos\theta &= \cos\theta \\[5pt] 2\cos\theta &= 1 \\[5pt] \cos\theta &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{align*}

This gives us two solutions for $\theta \in [-\pi,\pi]\mathbin{:}$ \[ \theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{\pi}{3} \]

To determine which is the inner function and which is the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

The arrow

  • enters the region through the inner function $r=1-\cos\theta,$ and

  • leaves through the outer function $r=\cos\theta.$

To find the area, we use the formula

\[ A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \Big( \big[ {\color{blue}\text{outer}} \big]^2 - \big[ {\color{brown}\text{inner}} \big]^2 \Big) \:\textrm{d}\theta, \]

where

$\qquad$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{3}, \quad$ and $\quad \theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} A &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3} \left( ({\color{blue}\cos\theta})^2 - ({\color{brown}1-\cos\theta})^2 \right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3} \left( \cos^2\theta - (1-2\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta)\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3} \left( 2\cos\theta - 1 \right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(2\sin\theta-\theta\right)\, \Bigg|_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\left(2\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\left(2\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\left(\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)-\left(-\sqrt{3}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}}. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Area of the Region Bounded by Two Polar Curves

question.text: Find the total area of the shaded region that lies between the polar curves $r=3+2\cos(5\theta)$ and $r=3,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Consider the rightmost petal, oriented along the $x$-axis. First, we find the values of $\theta$ for which the two curves intersect: \begin{align*} 3+2\cos(5\theta) &= 3 \\[5pt] \cos(5\theta) &= 0 \end{align*}

This gives us two solutions for $5\theta \in [-\pi,\pi]\mathbin{:}$ \[ 5\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta= -\dfrac{\pi}{10}, \dfrac{\pi}{10} \]

To determine which is the inner function and which is the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

The arrow

  • enters the region through the inner function $r=3,$ and

  • leaves through the outer function $r=3+2\cos(5\theta).$

To find the area, we use the formula

\[ A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \Big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{outer}} \big]^2 - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{inner}} \big]^2 \Big) \:\textrm{d}\theta, \]

where

$\qquad$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{10}, \quad$ and $\quad \theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{10}.$

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} A_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/10}^{\pi/10} \left( ({\color{brown}3+2\cos(5\theta)})^2 - ({\color{blue}3})^2 \right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/10}^{\pi/10} \left( 9+12\cos(5\theta) + 4\cos^2(5\theta) - 9 \right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/10}^{\pi/10} \left(12\cos(5\theta) + 4\cos^2(5\theta)\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/10}^{\pi/10} \left(12\cos(5\theta)+2(1+\cos(10\theta)) \right) \:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{12}{5}\sin(5\theta) + 2\theta + \dfrac{1}{5}\sin(10\theta) \right]_{-\pi/10}^{\pi/10} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(\dfrac{12}{5}+\dfrac{12}{5}\right) + \left(\dfrac{\pi}{5}+\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right) + 0 \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{12}{5}+\dfrac{\pi}{5}. \end{align*}

Finally, the total shaded area is \[ A = 5A_1 = 5\left( \dfrac{12}{5}+\dfrac{\pi}{5} \right)= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{12+\pi}. \]
